# EX09 Project: COMP110 Track Recommendation - Challenge Questions as Tailored Practice

## Using class survey data, we analyzed the relationship between coding experience and perceived difficulty of COMP110. 

This analysis used three primary variables to analyze difficulty: prior coding experience, explicit difficulty ratings, and hours spent working online. Cumulatively, it could be argued that this analysis supports the claim that students could benefit from extra credit or tiered-structure assingments in addition to the mandatory baseline assignments for the entire classThe box plot demonstrates that students with less than one year of coding experience rate the course difficulty significantly higher than those with greater than 7-12 months of coding experience. Additionally, students who have over two years of coding experience express low difficulty ratings which indicate a need for more challenging content. 

<img width="505" height="483" alt="876a3c16-b2a9-4d1b-9700-2396fde4c64c" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a8be5cf7-9af3-4343-a12f-afdcf4361f86" />

The count plot supports finding further, showing remarkably higher and clustered difficulty results in the range of 4-6. Conversely, experienced coders, while much fewer in numbers, tended to cluster from 2-5. 

<img width="730" height="482" alt="e77f5bd2-5cc2-4b28-9b39-39775d61f044" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7d4ba28a-57f8-4f58-8560-ab6fcf001fd2" />

The strip plot demonstrates that inexperienced coders who find the course difficult are  clustered around the 5-10 hour range for time spent working online. Conversely, more experienced coders who find the course easier spend far less time working online, indicating that COMP 110 might not be challenging enough for students who have a background in Python.

<img width="740" height="485" alt="d3403a53-72eb-4742-a2b6-cac67f6d037d" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/278f48ef-1d76-47c5-8392-2d6332d0c132" />

This analysis could be strengthened by creating a difficulty rating that is stratified to student experience. This could prove to be a far more precise measurement when examining the relationship between difficulty and prior experience. Additionally, a survey could directly ask students who took this course whether they would be interested in implementing a structure like this.  

Our claim does not have its drawbacks. Teaching assistants will have to grade more work, and extra credit incentives may overreward experienced students who have more time to rather than those who are overloaded with other coursework. Ultimately, the introduction of these new challenge questions runs into issues of time conservation, both for students and instructors. Nevertheless, this analysis ultimately endorses the claim that students could benefit from extra credit or tiered-structure assingments in addition to the mandatory baseline assignments for the entire class.
